newsitem.title: MEXICO: U.S. invites more Mexican oil imports.
newsitem.headline: U.S. invites more Mexican oil imports.

text.p: The United States welcomes greater crude oil imports from Mexico as part of a move to diversify crude sources to offset price shocks, a senior U.S. energy official said on Tuesday.

The United States is seeking "more diverse supply to offset shocks" in world crude prices by drawing more equally from its four principal suppliers, Canada, Venezuela, Mexico and Saudi Arabia, he said.
Latin America has been sharply increasing its share of the U.S. oil market for more than a decade and Mexico, together with Canada and Guatemala, showed the largest gains last year.
"The advantage of Mexico is its proximity to U.S. markets," the official, who declined to be named, told Reuters in a phone interview.

The official, a senior energy policy advisor, is part of President Clinton's first state visit to Mexico. U.S. Energy Secretary Federico Pena and his Mexican counterpart Jesus Reyes Heroles talked in Spanish for two and a half hours as part of the annual Binational Commission meetings held here on Monday.
The two were expected to cover three main areas: environment, foreign investment in Mexico's energy sector and security of supply issues.
"If you look at what is happening in energy markets all over the world, people are trading with closer suppliers to lower transportation costs as a function of greater competition."

Mexico supplies the United States with about 1.2 million barrels per day (bpd) of crude, the department of energy said in a statement. About 82 percent of Mexico's crude exports went to North America in March.
"As the demand for energy grows in our hemisphere, Mexico's resources will become increasingly important to securing our energy future."

The official called imminent Mexican crude deals with refiners in the U.S. West Coast "a good thing." However, a fixed contract scheme and some inflexibility of state oil and gas monopoly Petroleos Mexicanos (Pemex) has detracted some buyers, the official noted.
Competition for marketing crude has stiffened as Venezuela and Mexico boosted production this year and demand lulled amid a mild winter in key U.S. regions.
Pemex chairman Adrian Lajous has acknowledged stiff competition, though the company's traders deny rumors of offering discounts in the form of storage and advance deliveries.
Mexico has also been aggressively seeking to diversify its clients, specifically eyeing the U.S. West Coast, the Far East and boosting trade with Europe.
